newsitem.title: PERU: Victorious Peru works to sweep aside raid charges.
newsitem.headline: Victorious Peru works to sweep aside raid charges.

text.p: Peru sought on Monday to capitalise on its successful military strike against Marxist rebel hostage-takers and quash lingering criticism of human rights abuses in the raid and its aftermath.

"Everyone has applauded the government's decision and the way 72 people were rescued so cleanly and professionally," Justice Minister Carlos Hermoza Moya said. "We must not question the ever-so-clean and so beautiful way in which our men (soldiers) have given up their lives ... to save the highly valuable lives of 72 hostages."
Despite the death of one captive -- Judge Carlos Giusti, who bled to death after the attack -- the government claims the rescue achieved its goal because all 72 were freed alive.

Hermoza was the latest in a line of senior officials, including President Alberto Fujimori, to reject claims that two rebels were captured and executed during the raid and that families were kept away from the rebels' bodies afterwards.

Those reports have threatened to tarnish the acclaim Peru has received from around the world for a military strike hailed as one of the great rescue operations. All 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels and two commandos were slain on Tuesday when 140 commandos exploded through walls and tunnels to end Latin America's longest hostage siege.
Hermoza rejected demands from the influential Lima chamber of lawyers for an investigation into why Giusti's life was not saved with the application of a tourniquet.

While armed forces were reviewing their strategy to flush out the remaining 200-odd MRTA fighters in Peru's remote eastern jungle zone, the government moved to silence the group's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco, who is based in Hamburg, Germany, local media reported.

Velazco, whose public statements and maintenance of an MRTA Internet website were a constant irritation to the government during the four-month crisis, has been threatening reprisals from the MRTA to avenge Tuesday's attack.

The German government on Monday called on the government of Hamburg to ban his political activity following reports that Peru's Foreign Ministry had formally requested a cancellation of his political asylum status.
"I don't understand how there are countries who put up with these individuals who from abroad perform a role so disastrous to Peru," Hermoza said.

Fujimori, buoyed by soaring popularity and plaudits from around the world for the raid, continued on Monday a series of triumphant public appearances and media interviews. Over the weekend he led Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda around the 3,000-year-old Chavin de Huantar tunnel complex in Peru's Andes that inspired the tunnels under the residence from which troops burst out to overwhelm the MRTA.

Earlier, Fujimori had led cameras through the military's tunnels before emerging into the building to inspect the corpses of the rebels and the debris from the battle. He was to attend the inauguration with Thor Heyerdahl of an expedition depicting the Norwegian explorer's epic 1947 voyage that crossed from the Pacific.

Japan, meanwhile, insisted that it was no pushover in the face of terrorism. "Our country had been described generally as a country that is weak in the face of terrorism and that when threatened was always willing to pay," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told a parliamentary dinner in Canberra.
"But we also showed this time that when hostages are taken we do not just pay, follow the demands of the terrorists and expose Japanese lives to crisis," he said.
